segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika closed with a half-golden mongoose and a family's handful of flour. In between, the epic tells of the elders' deaths in the forest and the end of Krishna's people. Your line was atithi devo bhava: the guest is God.

The news from Dwaraka reaches Hastinapura: Krishna is gone, and his clan has destroyed itself. Yudhishthira makes up his mind in one sentence, in Ganguli's telling: time is cooking all creatures. It's time to go. He crowns Parikshit, the child who was born without breath, now grown, and puts the kingdom in others' care. Then the five brothers and Draupadi take off their jewelry, put on the plain clothes of forest hermits, and walk out through the gates. The city follows a little way, weeping, and turns back. One companion does not turn back. A dog.
screen: `NEWS FROM DWARAKA.` → `PARIKSHIT IS CROWNED.` → `SIX WALK OUT, AND A DOG.`

segments.voice: This is the Mahaprasthanika, the book of the great departure. The Pandavas walk east first: Yudhishthira leads, then Bhima, Arjuna, the twins, Draupadi, and the dog behind them all. They reach the sea, and a figure stands in their path, tall as a mountain: Agni, the god of fire. He speaks to Arjuna. Remember the great bow Gandiva? Agni brought it to Arjuna long ago, from Varuna, lord of the waters. Its work is finished; it belongs to Varuna; give it back. And Arjuna, who carried it through the whole war, throws it into the waves and walks on unarmed. Here's the teaching. Hindu tradition maps a life in four stages: the student, the householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller who hands the household on, and sannyasa, the renouncer who sets everything down. Many teachers read this morning as those last stages acted out: the kingdom to Parikshit, the jewels off at the gate, the bow back to the god it came from. The Isha Upanishad opens the same way: all this belongs to the Lord, so enjoy it by letting it go. That's why many Hindu elders still hand on jewelry, duties and the family puja, and set out on pilgrimage. Not as an ending. As the next stage. Then they walk on around the edge of the world, toward Meru. And the dog keeps coming.
screen: `MAHAPRASTHANIKA: THE GREAT DEPARTURE` · `AGNI STANDS AT THE SEA` · `THE BOW GOES INTO THE WAVES` · `FOUR STAGES OF LIFE` · then, large: `VANAPRASTHA: HAND IT ON, GIVE IT BACK`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind one thing you're known for, a skill, a role, a title. When Hindus make offerings into a sacred fire, each one is often followed by the words idam na mama: this is not mine. Breathe in and thank your gift for its work; breathe out and say silently, idam na mama, and notice what's left when it's not in your grip. If you don't pray, just say: this was never only mine.
Mahaprasthanika. The book of the great departure: five brothers, Draupadi and a dog walk out of the city, and Arjuna gives his bow back to the sea.
Your line: vanaprastha, hand it on, give it back. The dog is still following. Day eight hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: The Mahaprasthanika Parva tells the Pandavas' final walk; Hindus hear it in recitations of the epic, and the image of the brothers, Draupadi and the dog walking toward the Himalayas is often painted and retold.
